title: Seashells on mountaintops
teaches: How loose mud becomes layers of rock, and how to read their order

blocks.text: For centuries, people in Malta and Tuscany dug pointed, glossy stones out of the hillsides. Known as *glossopetrae*, or tongue stones, they were sold as charms against poison.[^tongues] Their origin was an open question, though the prevailing view was that they grew directly inside the rock, much as crystals do.

In October 1666, fishermen near Livorno caught an enormous great white shark. Ferdinando II de' Medici, the Grand Duke of Tuscany, had its head sent to Florence for dissection by a young Danish anatomist at his court: Niels Stensen, known in Latin as **Steno**. When Steno examined the creature's teeth, he saw that they matched the tongue stones in every detail, down to the fine serrations along the cutting edges.

blocks.caption: Illustration of the shark's head from Steno's 1667 treatise.
A fossil tongue stone beside a modern shark's tooth, sharing the same shape and serrated edges.

blocks.text: Steno doubted that a stone could simply grow inside rock into the exact likeness of a tooth. Crystals grow with flat faces and regular angles, either pushing the surrounding matrix aside or filling open cavities. A tongue stone has the porous, curved root and sharp blade of an organic tooth, and it sits embedded in the rock with no sign of having forced its way in. Some beds held whole sets of them mixed with ordinary seashells.

Recognising the tongue stones as real teeth raised a harder mechanical puzzle: how does one solid object end up encased inside another solid, high on a hill far from the coast? Steno worked out a general principle. When one solid encloses another, whichever body impressed its surface onto the other must have been hard first. Because the rock takes the impression of the tooth, the tooth was already solid when the surrounding stone formed. The host rock must therefore have begun as loose **sediment**, the mud and sand that settle out of water, soft enough to bury a shed tooth before hardening into stone. And a bed of mud full of shark teeth was once the floor of the sea.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Tongue stones (*glossopetrae*) are fossilised sharks' teeth.
When one solid encloses another and takes its impression, the inner object hardened first; a fossil encased in stone shows the rock began as loose sediment.

blocks.text: Steno spent the next two years travelling through Tuscany, examining the hills that yielded the teeth. The rock was arranged in **layers**, or **strata** (singular *stratum*), stacked like the pages of a closed book.[^strata] Some strata were sandstone, composed of sand grains cemented together. Others were mudstone or shale, compacted from fine mud. Still others were limestone, formed largely of calcium carbonate derived from marine shells and skeletons, often preserving whole shells within the matrix.

He reasoned that each stratum had begun as loose sediment carried by rivers and dropped on the floor of a sea or lake where the current slackened. Because the water's energy varies over time, the sediment it drops varies too. A winter flood carries coarse sand out into a basin, while a long calm spell lets fine mud settle out of suspension. Each shift in conditions initiates a distinct bed.

As younger beds accumulate on top, the buried sediment turns to stone. The weight of the overlying column squeezes water from the pore spaces between the grains, packing them closer together. Meanwhile, mineral-rich groundwater seeping through the remaining pores precipitates fine crystals, usually quartz or calcite, that bind the grains like mortar. Given depth and time, a loose sandbank becomes sandstone.
A sea floor has its own topography of ridges and hollows. The model below shows what happens to the geometry of the beds as sediment settles over an uneven basin floor.

blocks.caption: A basin with an uneven, tilted floor filling with mud and sand.
blocks.task: Commit to a prediction, then add layers until the top levels out

blocks.text: Wherever there is even slight movement in the water, loose grains wash off the crests and collect in the depressions. Each successive layer fills the lows more thickly than it covers the highs, until the top of the deposit is nearly flat. Steno called this **original horizontality**: sedimentary strata are laid down horizontally, or very nearly so. Exceptions occur in specific environments. In dead-still water, a fine rain of sediment can drape evenly over a submarine hill; on the advancing front of a **delta**, the wedge of sediment built where a river meets standing water, beds settle at a primary slope. Both leave diagnostic textures that can be recognised in the field.

A companion principle follows from the same physics: **lateral continuity**. A sheet of sediment extends sideways in all directions until it either thins to nothing or abuts the margin of the basin that held the water. If a river later carves a valley through a stack of flat-lying strata, the severed edges of each bed will match across the gorge at the same elevation. In the Grand Canyon, individual formations can be followed by eye for tens of kilometres around every promontory.

blocks.caption: The Grand Canyon, where horizontal strata can be traced continuously from one wall to the other.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Sedimentary strata accumulate as grains settle out of water or air.
Compaction and mineral cementation turn buried sediment into rock.
Original horizontality: most sedimentary layers are deposited nearly flat.
Lateral continuity: a stratum extends sideways until it thins out or meets the edge of its basin.

blocks.text: Steno's best-known rule is the principle of **superposition**: in any sequence of strata that has not been overturned since it formed, the lowest bed was deposited first and the highest bed last. Lower is older. An exposed cliff face can therefore be read from the base upward as a chronological record.

A fourth rule, **cross-cutting relationships**, is already implicit in Steno's work and was later formalised by James Hutton at the end of the eighteenth century and Charles Lyell in the 1830s. Any geological feature that cuts across strata must be younger than the strata it interrupts. A fracture can only break rock that is already there, and molten rock can only intrude along a fissure after the host beds are in place.

The section below illustrates two kinds of cross-cutting feature. A **fault** is a fracture along which the rock on one side has slipped relative to the other, offsetting the beds. A **dike** is a sheet of once-molten rock that forced its way up through a fracture and solidified. The section also records a period of **erosion**: when rock is lifted above water level, rain, wind and rivers plane its upper surface down, and younger strata may later be deposited across the truncated beds.

blocks.caption: A cliff face exposing four sedimentary layers, a fault and an igneous dike.
blocks.task: Place the six geological events in order from oldest to youngest

blocks.text: Consider layer D in the completed cliff. Because it runs unbroken across the fault, the fault movement must have ended before D was laid down. Between the faulting and the deposition of D, erosion shaved the displaced blocks flat, creating a level surface for D to cover. The dike slices through every bed including D, making that intrusion the final event in the sequence. All six steps can be placed in unambiguous chronological order without reference to a single calendar date.

Where strata now stand steeply tilted, vertical, or buckled into waves, the principle of original horizontality tells us they were deformed after they settled. Tectonic forces in the crust compressed or tipped them long after the mud had turned to stone.

blocks.caption: Folded strata on a rocky coast, originally deposited as flat sheets on a sea floor and later buckled by compression.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Superposition: in an undisturbed sequence, lower strata are older than higher ones.
Cross-cutting relationships: any fault, intrusion or erosional surface is younger than the rocks it cuts.
An eroded surface buried beneath younger beds marks an interval when the older rock stood exposed and was worn down.
Tilted or folded strata were deformed after deposition.

blocks.text: These principles return us to the hills of Tuscany, where beds of rock packed with seashells and sharks' teeth crop out far inland. By Steno's rules, those beds were deposited as flat sheets of mud and sand on a sea floor. Today they lie hundreds of metres above the Mediterranean, and many of them dip at steep angles.

blocks.caption: Ordovician limestone from Ohio packed with marine brachiopod and bryozoan shells, now exposed far from any ocean.

blocks.text: Rocks laid down in the sea, known as **marine** strata, now form high dry land, which requires either that the sea once stood higher or that the crust itself moved. In 1669 Steno published a compact Latin treatise whose full title states the general problem he had set out to solve: *On a solid body naturally contained within a solid*.[^prodromus] In it he reconstructed the geological history of Tuscany in six stages: horizontal strata accumulated beneath a universal sea; the waters withdrew while subterranean currents and vapours hollowed out great caverns beneath the beds; the cavern roofs collapsed, leaving the strata tilted and broken; the sea returned to deposit a younger set of horizontal beds across the rubble; and the cycle of undermining and collapse repeated once more.

Steno compressed all six stages into the few thousand years of the biblical chronology accepted across seventeenth-century Europe. Yet his stratigraphic rules do not depend on that timescale. They establish the relative order of events while remaining silent on how long each stage lasted. How much time is actually recorded in a thick pile of strata remained an open question for another century, and later lessons will return to it.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Marine fossils embedded in inland rocks demonstrate that those strata formed on a sea floor before being left high on land.
Steno's rules establish the relative sequence of geological events, independent of their absolute ages or durations.

blocks.caption: Six questions on reading rock layers
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: In this view of the Grand Canyon, which strata were deposited first?
choices: The lowest beds, down near the river
The beds forming the upper rim
All the beds formed at the same time
items.why: By superposition, undisturbed strata accumulate from the bottom up, so the lowest beds are the oldest. The Colorado River has cut downward through the stack, exposing the sequence in chronological order.

items.ask: Were these coastal strata deposited in their present contorted shape?
choices: No; they settled as flat sheets and were folded later
Yes; they draped over an already folded sea floor
items.why: Loose sediment settles into hollows until its upper surface is nearly horizontal. Tight chevron folds like these require the rock to have been compressed after it hardened.

items.ask: Why did Steno reject the idea that tongue stones grew inside the rock like crystals?
choices: Their anatomy matched a shark's teeth in detail, and they lacked the flat faces and geometry of crystals
They were only ever found near the modern shoreline
They were harder and glossier than the surrounding stone
items.why: Crystals grow with planar faces and constant interfacial angles. Tongue stones had the curved root, cutting blade and marginal serrations of an organic tooth, and they had impressed their shape into the surrounding sediment.

items.ask: An igneous dike cuts through strata A and B, but terminates cleanly at the base of stratum C, which lies unbroken on top of B. Which of the three features is youngest?
items.why: Because the dike cuts A and B, it must be younger than both. Because stratum C overlies the truncated top of the dike without being cut or baked by it, C was deposited after the dike had already intruded and cooled.

items.ask: A limestone bed high on an inland hill is packed with fossil seashells throughout its thickness. What can you conclude from this?
choices: The rock accumulated as sediment on a sea floor and now stands above sea level
A brief flood washed loose shells up onto the hill
The shells grew inside the rock after the hill formed
items.why: Because the shells are encased throughout the solid rock matrix, they were buried in marine sediment before it lithified. A passing overland flood would leave at most a thin surface scatter of shells rather than thick beds of solid limestone.

items.ask: Why do sedimentary layers generally start out nearly horizontal, even when deposited over an irregular basin floor?
choices: Currents and gravity sweep loose grains off the highs into the lows until the surface levels out
The hydrostatic weight of the overlying water presses the mud flat
Sea floors are already flat before sediment arrives
items.why: Gravity and bottom currents carry loose grains downslope into depressions, so each successive bed thickens in the hollows and thins over the highs until the top of the fill is nearly level.

learned: A fossil encased in stone hardened before the rock around it, showing that the host rock began as loose sediment.
Buried sediment turns into sedimentary rock through compaction and mineral cementation.
Sedimentary strata are deposited nearly flat (original horizontality) and extend sideways until they thin out or meet a basin margin (lateral continuity).
In an undisturbed pile, lower strata are older (superposition), and any fault, dike or erosion surface is younger than the beds it cuts.
Marine fossils in mountain rocks show that those strata formed on ancient sea floors before ending up high on land.

tongues.title: Tongue stones as medicine
tongues.text: In Maltese folklore they were the tongues of vipers turned to stone when Saint Paul was shipwrecked on the island. Across Europe, wealthy diners suspended them from coral branches in silver mounts or dipped them into wine to sweat out or neutralise poison, and apothecaries sold them ground into powder well into the eighteenth century.

strata.title: Stratum and stratigraphy
strata.text: A **stratum** (plural *strata*, from the Latin for a spread-out covering or paving) is a single distinct layer of sedimentary rock. The branch of geology concerned with rock strata and their chronological order is **stratigraphy**.

prodromus.title: Steno's Prodromus
prodromus.text: The treatise is usually cited as the *Prodromus* (*De solido intra solidum naturaliter contento dissertationis prodromus*), Latin for a preliminary discourse to a longer work. Steno never wrote the full treatise. Having converted from Lutheranism to Catholicism in 1667, he was ordained a priest in 1675, became a missionary bishop in northern Germany, and died in self-imposed poverty in 1686.
